newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ on brink of new govt after two-month wait.
newsitem.headline: NZ on brink of new govt after two-month wait.

text.p: New Zealand was poised for a new government after two months of deadlock on Tuesday as MPs from the nationalist New Zealand First party met to choose a coalition partner.
The party's 17 MPs, all but four of them new to parliament, will decide whether to keep the conservative National Party in office or restore centre-left Labour to power after six years in opposition.
Over weeks of negotiation, NZ First leader Winston Peters has thrashed out separate secret deals with National and Labour to put before his party for a decision on Tuesday.
Peters, the party's dominant figure, told reporters he would not express a personal preference and would let the caucus of MPs decide.
"It's going to be a party and caucus decision...They will make the decision themselves," he said.
Peters formed NZ First after being sacked from cabinet by Prime Minister Jim Bolger in 1991, but says he will not allow bad blood to influence the choice.

New Zealand First won all five seats reserved for Maoris -- previously a stronghold of the Labour Party -- in the October 12 election. The influence of the Maori MPs is seen as crucial to the party's choice.
"Yes, my people have an expectation of me to go Labour," said Tutekawa Wyllie, MP for one of the Maori seats.

Another, Tukuroirangi Morgan, told reporters thousands of people in his constituency had deserted Labour for NZ First "because of the Labour Party's apathy and mediocrity. Maori people were sick and tired of being marginalised".

He added: "I've gone back to the people and they have said to me in some respects that the Labour Party is the preference but...it's an even race. We'll weigh up the decision on what will benefit Maori."
Maori, who represent 13 percent of the population, make up a disadvantaged socio-economic group with poorer health, lower life expectancy and higher unemployment than whites.
Both Labour and NZ First want to scrap a NZ$1 billion (US$700 million) cap imposed by National on compensation for ancestral Maori lands that were seized by colonial settlers.

National has presided over the highest economic growth in a generation, but lost ground during the election campaign as Labour and other parties attacked its record on health and education and promised greater funding.

National's campaign was largely based on the promise of further tax cuts next year, but leaks from the coalition talks suggest it may be willing to compromise on the timing in order to accommodate NZ First's spending priorities.

NZ First fought the election on an economic strategy of export-led growth and promises to put ordinary New Zealanders' interests above those of foreigners and big business. It favours a 24.9 percent limit on foreign holdings in strategic assets.
National has 44 seats in the new 120-member parliament and Labour 37, with New Zealand First on 17.
A Labour-NZ First coalition would need support from the left-wing Alliance, which confirmed on Tuesday it would back such a government on confidence issues.
